paragraphs: Tree-based language-model reasoning explores several possible continuations and may return to earlier branches. Keeping the attention key–value states for all these partial paths can consume substantial memory. ArborKV addresses this storage bottleneck by using the structure of the search to decide which cached information deserves immediate space.

The central observation is that upcoming generation mainly needs the current branch and its ancestors. Other subtrees are less likely to be used soon, although backtracking means they cannot simply become inaccessible. ArborKV combines a lightweight estimate of cache value with a policy that allocates memory according to the tree. It removes selected token entries and restores needed information lazily when a branch is revisited.

On the reported Tree-of-Thoughts reasoning benchmarks, ArborKV reduces peak cache memory by up to roughly fourfold while retaining accuracy close to keeping the full cache. This makes larger searches feasible within a fixed device budget, including configurations that otherwise exhaust memory. The contribution is therefore a way to support broader or deeper reasoning searches by matching cache retention to expected branch reuse.
icml-2026-arborkv-structure-aware-kv-cac.tldr: ArborKV uses reasoning-tree structure to reduce peak KV-cache memory by up to roughly fourfold while preserving near-full-retention accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making when losses can occasionally take unusually large values. Such heavy tails complicate learning because extreme observations can distort estimates. The goal is to control regret—the accumulated cost of learning relative to a comparator—both when losses behave stochastically and when they are adversarial.

When transition probabilities are known, HT-FTRL-OM optimizes occupancy measures, which describe how a policy distributes visits across states and actions. It combines regularized learning with loss estimators that skip observations. Its adversarial regret scales as T^(1/α), apart from logarithmic factors, while stochastic regret grows logarithmically. These guarantees let the same method benefit from favorable environments without abandoning adversarial protection.

For unknown transitions, HT-FTRL-UOB adds a pessimistic skipping estimator. Under the stated truncative nonnegativity condition, its adversarial bound includes both T^(1/α) and a square-root-of-T term, with logarithmic factors suppressed; its stochastic bound grows as log²(T). The analysis separates uncertainty about transitions from heavy-tailed estimation errors and skipping bias. This separation explains how the guarantees accommodate both difficult loss distributions and incomplete knowledge of the environment.
icml-2026-best-of-both-worlds-for-heavy-.tldr: Two algorithms provide adaptive regret guarantees for heavy-tailed decision processes with known or, under a stated distributional condition, unknown transitions.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate tokens in flexible orders, making the choice of which predictions to accept an important part of inference. Existing decoding methods often judge predictions using confidence or entropy from the current step. The paper argues that this immediate view can favor choices that do not remain coherent as generation develops.

Coherent Contextual Decoding, or CCD, instead uses contexts from earlier decoding steps to approximate the marginal distribution of token predictions. Looking across this history reduces dependence on a single context and helps reject less promising generation paths early. The authors also establish a theoretical equivalence between this mechanism and measuring historical consistency through conditional mutual information between contexts and predictions.

Experiments on Dream and LLaDA report improvements in both inference speed and performance across diverse benchmarks. CCD also loses less performance than the compared methods when decoding becomes highly parallel. These findings suggest that historical agreement can guide efficient generation more effectively than immediate confidence alone in the evaluated settings, especially when many token decisions are made together.
icml-2026-beyond-confidence-adaptive-and.tldr: CCD uses historical decoding contexts to improve diffusion-language-model coherence, speed, and performance under parallel generation.

paragraphs: Motion-language retrieval connects descriptions with matching human movements. A common approach compares a representation of an entire motion sequence with a representation of the entire text. That can obscure which body joints or portions of the movement correspond to particular words, weakening the treatment of detailed descriptions.

The proposed Pyramidal Shapley-Taylor framework breaks motion into two complementary parts: segments across time and joints across the body. It progressively learns correspondences between these motion components and text tokens. The progression follows a hierarchy from individual joint dynamics through coherent motion segments to an understanding of the whole sequence.

This organization matters because a useful match depends on both local details and how those details fit together. The framework is designed to preserve these relationships instead of relying exclusively on a single global comparison. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, alongside precise correspondence between motion components and their associated text tokens. The stated findings support hierarchical, fine-grained alignment as a stronger basis for retrieval in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-beyond-global-alignment-fine-g.tldr: Pyramidal Shapley-Taylor learning improves motion-language retrieval by progressively aligning body joints and temporal segments with text tokens.

paragraphs: Designing a protein for a specified biochemical function requires more than producing an amino-acid sequence: the sequence must also support a suitable folded structure. The paper addresses this joint requirement in de novo design, where generation does not depend on evolutionary templates. Existing direct sequence generation and separated structure–sequence approaches can struggle to satisfy both goals together.

CodeFP tackles the problem by decoding sequence tokens and structure tokens simultaneously. It enriches the representation of the requested function using local structures associated with function, giving the model more structurally informative guidance. It also adds auxiliary supervision about function to reduce training ambiguity caused by the one-to-many mapping from structures to tokens.

The reported experiments show average improvements of 6.1% in functional consistency and 3.2% in foldability over the strongest baseline. These results support the value of coordinating sequence and structure generation rather than handling their requirements separately. The contribution is a model that links functional guidance to structural generation while explicitly training toward both desired function and the ability to fold.
icml-2026-co-generative-de-novo-function.tldr: CodeFP jointly generates protein sequence and structure tokens, improving measured functional consistency and foldability over the strongest baseline.

paragraphs: Federated learning on graphs with textual attributes can use language models to interpret node information, but long texts and surrounding neighborhoods make this expensive. Compressing the graph into a smaller core reduces the workload. However, a fixed, one-time compression may fit clients poorly, and generated summaries can obscure the evidence behind predictions.

DANCE makes condensation an ongoing part of federated training. At each round, the latest global model helps refresh the compressed representation, allowing it to respond to the evolving model rather than remaining fixed. To support inspection, the method also stores local evidence packs that connect predictions to selected neighbors and specific spans of source text.

Across eight text-attributed graph datasets, the authors report a 2.33% accuracy improvement at an 8% condensation ratio, alongside 33.42% fewer tokens per condensed node than the compared federated baselines. The findings connect efficiency with two additional benefits: compression that adapts during training and records that expose its textual grounding. DANCE therefore treats condensation as both a computational decision and an inspectable learning process.
icml-2026-dance-dynamic-available-neighb.tldr: DANCE refreshes graph condensation during federated training and preserves source evidence, improving reported accuracy while reducing token use.

paragraphs: Language models used as evaluators can make systematic mistakes, so averaging their judgments need not recover the underlying average quality or win rate. This paper studies how to calibrate those judgments statistically. It compares direct corrections based on misclassification models with prediction-powered inference, which uses a small set of human labels to correct prediction residuals.

The authors place both approaches within a shared framework using semiparametric efficiency theory. They derive efficient estimators through explicit influence functions, mathematical tools that characterize how individual observations affect an estimate. This makes it possible to compare the uncertainty of the two correction strategies within a common theoretical treatment.

A central result identifies conditions under which prediction-powered estimators have strictly lower asymptotic variance than measurement-error corrections. That is a conditional advantage in large-sample precision, rather than a claim that one approach always wins. Simulations verify the theoretical findings, and a real-data example demonstrates the calibration methods through an open-source software package. The work provides a principled basis for choosing how to turn imperfect automated judgments into estimates of mean evaluation outcomes.
icml-2026-efficient-inference-for-noisy-.tldr: The paper unifies two ways to calibrate imperfect LLM judges and identifies when prediction-powered inference gives more precise estimates.

paragraphs: Adapting a general robot model to particular hardware often requires collecting demonstrations under a tight budget. This paper argues that maximizing variety by recording each condition only once can be self-defeating. Spreading demonstrations too thinly leaves estimation noise, even though the data cover more situations.

The authors formalize this tension by separating policy error into a density-related estimation term and a coverage-related extrapolation term. Their analysis characterizes an interior optimum for the number of unique conditions under a fixed budget. Anchor-Centric Adaptation follows this reasoning in two stages: repeated demonstrations at core conditions first stabilize a policy skeleton, then additional data expand coverage toward high-risk boundaries.

The second stage uses teacher-forced error mining to identify where expansion is needed and constrained residual updates to adapt the policy. Real-robot experiments support the proposed coverage–density trade-off and show significantly better reliability and success rates than standard diverse sampling under the same budget. The practical implication is that strategic repetition and selective expansion can make limited demonstrations more useful than pursuing coverage alone.
icml-2026-escaping-the-diversity-trap-in.tldr: Anchor-Centric Adaptation combines repeated core demonstrations with targeted coverage expansion to improve robot adaptation under a fixed data budget.

paragraphs: Training a 3D variational autoencoder through rendered views avoids some losses associated with converting meshes into signed distance fields. But a rendered view directly supervises only visible geometry. Many latent voxels can therefore receive weak supervision while still consuming decoding and attention resources.

Focusing removes voxels inconsistent with a training view’s rendered depth before decoding. This concentrates computation on geometry relevant to that view. An adaptive zooming mechanism adjusts camera intrinsics to keep the active voxel count within a target range and strengthen fine-detail supervision. Training combines depth, normal, mask, and perceptual losses with sparse-voxel total variation and a brief truncated signed-distance-field warm-up to improve convergence and suppress holes.

On standard reconstruction benchmarks, the method improves Chamfer Distance and F-score over strong baselines while substantially reducing GPU memory use. The authors report training at 1024³ resolution with 512³ trunks using as little as 50 GB of VRAM. The result supports view-consistent sparsity as a practical way to devote high-resolution training resources to surface regions that actually contribute to the current rendered supervision.
icml-2026-focusing-view-consistent-spars.tldr: Focusing prunes view-inconsistent latent voxels before decoding, improving 3D reconstruction while reducing memory needed for high-resolution VAE training.

paragraphs: Combining color and depth information can help identify salient objects, but the two streams may differ substantially in reliability. When a noisy auxiliary stream exchanges information symmetrically with a stronger primary stream, noise can flow backward into the primary representation and accumulate through repeated refinement.

Hamiltonian Asymmetric Fusion treats this situation as directed refinement. The primary stream supplies guidance, while updates refine the auxiliary tokens and explicitly quantify auxiliary-induced perturbations of the primary representation. The refinement uses Hamiltonian-inspired dynamics with regularized momentum and gated driving. Global correlations are computed in the frequency domain using FFTs, and a shared learned spectral response emphasizes reliable frequency components.

A leaky momentum gate reduces the influence of stale updates across refinement steps. Together, these mechanisms are designed to make repeated fusion more controlled under modality imbalance. Experiments on six color-and-depth salient-object detection benchmarks report consistent gains and more gradual performance degradation when the auxiliary input is deliberately corrupted. The evidence supports asymmetric refinement for the stated setting where one modality is substantially noisier than the designated primary modality.
icml-2026-hamiltonian-asymmetric-fusion-.tldr: Hamiltonian Asymmetric Fusion uses directed, gated refinement to improve RGB–D object detection when the auxiliary modality is noisy.

paragraphs: An interactive scientific demonstration requires a model to combine scientific understanding with code that responds correctly to user interaction. Evaluating only written reasoning or static code misses this combined demand. InteractScience introduces a benchmark specifically for assessing the creation of complete interactive scientific applications.

Its evaluation framework combines two kinds of evidence. Programmatic functional tests check application logic, while visually grounded qualitative assessment examines rendering fidelity. These complementary checks address different parts of the task: whether the application behaves correctly and whether its visual presentation faithfully realizes the demonstration. Bringing them together makes the interface itself part of the scientific evaluation.

The authors evaluate 30 leading models across five disciplines and identify critical gaps in translating scientific reasoning into interactive interfaces. The finding concerns the combined capability, which cannot be captured fully by testing reasoning or coding in isolation. By standardizing this form of evaluation, InteractScience provides a basis for assessing progress toward more reliable scientific and educational applications generated by language models.
icml-2026-interactscience-programmatic-a.tldr: InteractScience combines functional tests and visual assessment to reveal gaps in models’ ability to build interactive scientific demonstrations.

paragraphs: Large generalized eigenvalue problems are computationally demanding across science and engineering. Contour-integral solvers offer an efficient, parallelizable approach, but their performance depends strongly on the integration contours they use. Choosing contours without useful knowledge of the eigenvalue distribution can increase computation and weaken numerical accuracy.

Deepcontour combines a learned prediction stage with a classical numerical solver. Its Eigen-Neural-Operator rapidly estimates information about the spectral distribution. A kernel density estimation module uses that information to construct suitable integration contours automatically. Those contours then guide the contour-integral solver toward the desired eigenvalues, giving the predictive model a specific role in configuring the numerical computation.

Across diverse scientific datasets, the framework achieves speedups of up to 5.63 times while maintaining the reported numerical rigor. The result shows how learned spectral priors can improve an important solver design choice without asking the predictor to perform the entire eigenvalue calculation. Its contribution is the connection between fast distributional prediction, systematic contour construction, and the accuracy-preserving work of the classical solver.
icml-2026-learning-guided-integration-co.tldr: Deepcontour uses learned spectral priors to construct integration contours, accelerating generalized eigensolvers by up to 5.63 times.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks hidden features that describe how data are generated through causal relationships. This paper studies a linear setting: latent features follow a linear structural causal model, and observed measurements are linear mixtures of those features. The challenge is to recover interpretable causal features from those mixtures.

Existing approaches often require restrictive information, such as interventions on individual hidden variables, or strong assumptions about feature and measurement-noise distributions. The proposed algorithm weakens requirements on both variation across environments and the underlying distributions. It still recovers the latent causal features up to an equivalence class, meaning the result identifies a permitted family of representations rather than necessarily one unique representation.

The authors test the algorithm using synthetic experiments and an interpretability analysis of large language models. They report better finite-sample performance than competing methods and evidence of potential for using causality to understand AI systems. The contribution expands the conditions under which recovery is possible within the specified linear formulation, while preserving an explicit qualification on what recovery identifies.
icml-2026-linear-causal-representation-l.tldr: The proposed linear causal-representation algorithm recovers latent features up to an equivalence class under weaker environmental and distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: LoKiFormer addresses two proposed sources of inefficiency in language-model pretraining. Standard self-attention has no explicit preference for nearby patterns, which can lead to redundant modeling of local sequence information. Mixture-of-experts architectures also tie stored knowledge to computational pathways, limiting flexibility in how broader knowledge is accessed.

The architecture adds two specialized components to a standard decoder. Local Fusion Attention uses convolutional fusion to capture nearby patterns before attention works with the resulting representations. The Knowledge Memory Module stores global knowledge in learned key–value slots that can be addressed directly. This separates the role of retaining knowledge from the computational paths used to process a sequence.

Together, the modules provide dedicated mechanisms for local information within the current sequence and global knowledge stored in model parameters. Experiments report 1.33-times faster pretraining convergence than the baseline models. The finding supports the proposed division of architectural responsibilities in the evaluated setting: local structure receives explicit processing, while learned global knowledge becomes directly accessible through a separate memory component.
icml-2026-lokiformer-locality-aware-atte.tldr: LoKiFormer combines convolution-enhanced attention with addressable knowledge memory and reports 1.33-times faster pretraining convergence.

paragraphs: Loop invariants describe properties that remain true as a program repeats a loop, making them useful for verification. For programs that manipulate memory, these properties must often describe the shape of heap-allocated structures and their layout. Existing methods handle numerical relationships more successfully than these structural properties.

MALICE starts from the hypothesis that source code leaves memory-state evolution too implicit for reliable invariant generation. It gives a language model symbolic execution traces that explicitly expose those transitions. A first stage uses guided, multistep reasoning over the traces to propose invariants. A second stage iteratively corrects the candidates using feedback from verification tools.

The design connects two kinds of support: traces make the relevant behavior visible, and verification feedback helps refine proposed properties. On LIG-MM+, a benchmark containing common operations on typical memory structures, MALICE substantially outperforms existing approaches. The reported result supports grounding invariant generation in explicit memory transitions and checking the resulting candidates, rather than relying on source-code interpretation alone.
icml-2026-malice-memory-aware-loop-invar.tldr: MALICE combines symbolic memory traces with verification feedback to improve loop-invariant generation for memory-manipulating programs.

paragraphs: Identifying an interpretable component inside a language model does not by itself explain which training examples caused it to develop. Mechanistic Data Attribution addresses this origin question. The framework uses influence functions to trace interpretable model units back to particular training samples.

Experiments on the Pythia family test those attributions through interventions. Removing or augmenting a small fraction of highly influential samples significantly changes the emergence of interpretable attention heads, whereas random interventions show no effect in the reported experiments. The analysis identifies repetitive structural material, including LaTeX and XML, as a catalyst for these mechanisms.

Interventions aimed at induction-head formation also produce concurrent changes in in-context learning capability. The authors present this as direct causal evidence for the hypothesized functional connection between induction heads and in-context learning. They additionally build a data-augmentation pipeline that consistently accelerates circuit convergence across model scales. Together, the findings connect training-data selection to internal mechanism development and show a concrete way to influence that development through targeted data changes.
icml-2026-mechanistic-data-attribution-t.tldr: Mechanistic Data Attribution identifies training samples whose targeted modification causally changes interpretable heads and associated in-context learning behavior.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine shared learning with differences between clients. Those differences can involve several overlapping levels of similarity, making a fixed clustering or a single form of personalization too restrictive. This paper models client relationships through global, subgroup, and client-specific components.

Federated Multi-level Additive Modeling, or FeMAM, learns shareable models at several levels and adds their contributions to construct personalized predictors. Its structure can grow and be pruned during training, allowing the organization of shared knowledge to adapt. This reduces dependence on knowing task boundaries or choosing a fixed grouping structure in advance.

Maintaining multiple models could increase training cost, so FeMAM activates only a small subset at one level at a time. Experiments report that it effectively approximates complex patterns of non-identically distributed client data and consistently outperforms representative clustered and personalized federated-learning baselines. The results support using several granularities of sharing together: clients can benefit from broad commonalities, more selective subgroup knowledge, and individual adjustments within the same additive formulation.
icml-2026-personalized-additive-modeling.tldr: FeMAM builds personalized federated predictors from dynamically adapted global, subgroup, and client-specific model components.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation depends on external documents, so corrupted search results can influence the answers it produces. Dynamic web search adds another difficulty: legitimate information also changes over time. A defense must resist attacks while remaining responsive to real updates, without requiring an ever-growing archive of historical documents.

RADAR formulates reliable context selection as an energy-minimization problem on a graph. It solves that formulated optimization exactly using Max-Flow Min-Cut. A Bayesian memory node carries a recursively updated belief state across time, providing historical information without retaining the raw documents that produced it.

This compressed memory is intended to balance resistance to malicious changes with adaptation to genuine knowledge shifts. Experiments on a new dynamic dataset report better robustness and response quality than the baselines, with minimal storage overhead. The exactness claim concerns solving the graph optimization; the evidence for improved defense comes from the experiments. The combined contribution is a context-selection mechanism that incorporates evolving historical beliefs while keeping its memory requirements small.
icml-2026-radar-defending-rag-dynamicall.tldr: RADAR combines exact graph-based context selection with compact Bayesian memory to defend RAG against changing retrieval corruption.

paragraphs: A robot following a long instruction can make locally plausible choices that undermine eventual completion. This paper proposes viewing such instruction drift as systematic sampling error. Its account centers on highly probable local choices that enter irreversible traps and cut off successful longer-term trajectories.

Context-Aware Power Sampling, or CAPS, addresses this at inference time without updating model parameters. It uses power distributions to sharpen probabilities over whole trajectories and supports lookahead search through the model’s conditional trajectory distribution. An additional controller uses a signal-to-noise measure to detect drift risk and trigger adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo search only when that risk is detected.

The intended benefit is selective use of extra computation: routine decisions can remain fast, while risky situations receive more search. Experiments on RoboTwin, Simpler-WindowX, and Libero-long report substantial improvements over strong baselines, including OpenVLA and TACO. These results support adaptive inference-time computation for longer-horizon robotic control in the evaluated settings. The sampling-error explanation is the paper’s proposed account of drift, while the benchmark improvements establish the reported effectiveness of its intervention.
icml-2026-rethinking-instruction-drift-a.tldr: CAPS detects instruction-drift risk and selectively searches future trajectories, improving long-horizon robot performance without parameter updates.

paragraphs: Rotating a panoramic image in three dimensions changes how its content is represented, making embedded watermarks difficult to recover reliably. This paper treats panoramas as signals on a sphere and builds descriptors whose values remain unchanged under the rotation group SO(3). The goal is to obtain rotation robustness from mathematical structure.

Spherical harmonic coefficients change predictably under rotation, but simple invariant summaries can discard directional information and constrain watermark capacity. The proposed construction couples higher-order representations through tensor products and projects the result onto the rotation-invariant component. This produces a third-order spherical bispectrum that preserves phase information while remaining strictly invariant to rotation.

The method embeds watermarks in higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients and reads them through invariant bispectral scalars. The authors prove the construction’s SO(3) invariance and report near-perfect experimental robustness to continuous rotations while maintaining high visual fidelity. These are complementary claims: the proof establishes an invariant representation, and the experiments show how effectively the watermarking system uses it. The approach connects richer spherical information with reliable extraction under arbitrary three-dimensional rotations.
icml-2026-rotation-invariant-spherical-w.tldr: A provably rotation-invariant spherical bispectrum enables panoramic watermark extraction with near-perfect experimental robustness to continuous 3D rotations.

paragraphs: Protein representations often emphasize amino-acid sequences or backbone geometry, leaving out detailed side-chain arrangements and local chemistry. SLAE learns a representation for each residue from its surrounding atoms. Its inputs consist only of atom types and interatomic geometry, grounding the representation in the local physical environment.

The framework trains an autoencoder with three objectives: reconstructing coordinates, recovering sequence information, and predicting energy. Combining these tasks encourages the latent representation to capture several aspects of the same atomic neighborhood. Geometry must be represented accurately enough for reconstruction, while the other objectives encourage chemically and energetically informative features.

The authors report high-fidelity all-atom reconstruction and state-of-the-art transfer performance across diverse downstream tasks. They also find that the latent space responds to chemical identity and environmental differences, supporting quantitative structural-quality assessment and smooth interpolation between conformations at all-atom resolution. The stated findings suggest that strictly local atomic neighborhoods can provide useful transferable protein features while retaining detailed information about structure and chemistry.
icml-2026-slae-strictly-local-all-atom-e.tldr: SLAE learns transferable protein representations from local all-atom geometry using reconstruction, sequence-recovery, and energy-prediction objectives.

paragraphs: Training language models with four-bit numbers can improve efficiency, but such limited precision makes it difficult to preserve training quality. TetraJet-v2 uses the NVFP4 format for activations, weights, and gradients throughout all linear layers. The paper identifies weight oscillation and outliers as two central obstacles to accurate training at this precision.

The method combines three responses. An unbiased double-block quantization scheme handles NVFP4 linear layers. OsciReset suppresses weight oscillation, while OutControl aims to retain accuracy for outlying values. Together, these components target both unstable weight behavior and the difficulty of representing unusually large values within a very compact numerical format.

The evaluation covers models up to 370 million parameters trained on as many as 212 billion tokens. TetraJet-v2 outperforms prior FP4 pretraining methods, reducing the performance gap to BF16 by an average of 51.3%, and delivers a 1.67-times end-to-end speedup over FP8. The results show a substantial narrowing of the accuracy gap rather than its elimination, alongside a measured training-speed benefit within the reported evaluation scale.
icml-2026-tetrajet-v2-accurate-nvfp4-tra.tldr: TetraJet-v2 targets weight oscillation and outliers to improve four-bit LLM training accuracy while achieving a 1.67-times speedup over FP8.

paragraphs: Cybersecurity research needs labeled traffic that reflects real malware behavior, but collecting it at scale is difficult. A malware sample may require particular environmental dependencies before it exhibits malicious behavior. Generic sandboxes can miss those requirements, while manually constructing suitable environments does not scale easily.

Threat2Traffic uses threat-intelligence documents to identify sample-specific dependencies and construct tailored environments for capturing traffic. Multiple agents deliberate over an evidence graph to resolve ambiguity in the source material. The environment-synthesis stage follows invariants and applies two layers of validation, checking both syntactic constraints and semantic requirements. These stages address different failure points: understanding the documented requirements and turning them into a working environment.

Evaluation on 1,077 samples spanning eight malware families achieves an 83.1% reproduction success rate. This provides empirical support for using structured agent collaboration and validated environment construction to generate realistic malware traffic at scale. The authors also release core source code and a traffic dataset. The contribution centers on making sample-specific environment reconstruction more systematic and usable for data collection.
icml-2026-threat2traffic-multi-agent-env.tldr: Threat2Traffic converts threat intelligence into validated, sample-specific environments, achieving 83.1% malware-behavior reproduction success in its evaluation.

paragraphs: Extra computation during language-model inference can include generating intermediate reasoning or sampling several candidate answers. Randomness helps these methods explore different possibilities, yet earlier theoretical analyses often assume deterministic decoding. This paper develops a framework that explicitly includes sampling and randomness in the analysis of test-time computation.

The authors study in-context linear regression as a controlled setting for the framework. They consider regression problems with both continuous and binary coefficients, and model decoding through noise injection and sampling. This creates a way to examine inference techniques while retaining the stochastic behavior that motivates their use in practical language models.

Numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings, and additional experiments on real-world tasks support the framework’s potential practical relevance. The contribution is presented as an initial step toward connecting mathematical analysis with stochastic inference, with linear regression serving as the central demonstration. Its significance lies in making randomness part of the theoretical object being studied, enabling analysis of how sampling participates in the benefits of extra inference-time computation.
icml-2026-towards-theoretical-understand.tldr: The paper introduces a stochastic framework for analyzing transformer test-time computation and demonstrates it through in-context linear regression.

paragraphs: Powerful video generators can supply detail for video super-resolution, but adapting them introduces a tension between visual richness and fidelity to the input. Real-world degradations can create artifacts, while strong generative behavior can compromise structural accuracy. WEVSR adapts a pretrained flow-matching video diffusion transformer to address these issues.

The method has two main components. A task-specific adaptation strategy uses timestep sampling and noise augmentation to improve detail restoration while maintaining structural stability. A lightweight front-end applies a multilevel discrete wavelet transform before the variational autoencoder’s encoder. This supplies explicit frequency information to the latent representation while keeping the pretrained decoder unchanged.

The combination targets both the restoration process and the representation of the degraded input. Wavelet-based guidance provides frequency structure, while the adaptation strategy controls how the pretrained generator is used for restoration. Experiments across multiple video super-resolution benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance against existing approaches. The findings support adapting large video generators through targeted training choices and a compact encoder addition to improve restoration quality.
icml-2026-wevsr-video-diffusion-generato.tldr: WEVSR combines task-specific diffusion adaptation with a wavelet-enhanced encoder to achieve reported state-of-the-art video super-resolution performance.
